body:
Great checklist. We run a 31-agent deployment (KinthAI, built on OpenClaw) and your P0 items are exactly right — but a few additions from harder-won experience:

**On Cost Guardrails: Pessimistic Allocation**

Per-agent daily caps are necessary but not sufficient. The failure mode is: agent starts an expensive operation, gets halfway through, hits the cap, and leaves the work in an inconsistent state. We use pessimistic allocation instead — deduct the *cost ceiling* before each LLM call, credit back the difference after. This means the agent never starts work it can't finish.

The budget hierarchy matters too: namespace → user → agent → conversation. A per-agent cap of $10/day doesn't help if one conversation within that agent is burning $8.

Details: [Your AI Agent Needs a Wallet](https://blog.kinthai.ai/agent-wallet-economic-models-autonomous-agents)

**On Circuit Breakers: Economic, Not Just Retry-Based**

Your "max 3 retries per task" is a good start, but the circuit breaker should also trip on spending rate. We use closed → half-open → open states:
- **Closed**: normal, spending within 1σ of rolling average
- **Half-open**: spending rate > 2σ, downgrade model tier (Opus → Sonnet → Haiku)
- **Open**: spending rate > 3σ or budget exhausted, emit budget-paused event

The half-open state is what prevents the "one stuck agent drains budget overnight" scenario you mentioned.

**On Context Budget: Smart Model Routing**

Our distribution: ~58% Haiku, ~31% Sonnet, ~11% Opus, giving a blended cost of ~$3.20/M tokens. An intent classifier at the gateway routes each task to the cheapest model that can handle it. This alone is a 5.2x cost advantage over always-Opus.

**P0 Addition: Memory Isolation**

Missing from the checklist: per-agent memory isolation. Without it, agents cross-contaminate each other's context. More on this: [Why Character.AI Forgets You](https://blog.kinthai.ai/why-character-ai-forgets-you-persistent-memory-architecture)

More on multi-agent production patterns: [What We Learned Running 221 Agents](https://blog.kinthai.ai/221-agents-multi-agent-coordination-lessons)

body:
The strongest control I have seen here is to treat every durable memory write as a promotion decision, not just as another text chunk to retrieve later.

A useful shape is:

- separate temporary observations from durable preferences, facts, and policy
- attach source, confidence, evidence count, TTL, consumer-agent scope, and rollback pointer to each promoted memory
- require explicit confirmation for high-impact preferences or anything that changes future authority
- keep negative evidence around too, so one poisoned page cannot silently override a long-running pattern
- make shared memories carry a maximum authority level, so a content-agent note can never become something an HR, finance, or deployment agent treats as policy

The three-times threshold idea is a good start, but I would pair it with memory type and authority boundaries. Otherwise repeated poison from the same compromised context can look exactly like evidence.
author: armorer-labs

body:
The promotion-as-decision framing is the right shape. Worth pushing on one more dimension: who is doing the promoting matters as much as what is being promoted.

The architecture I have been running for a few months treats memory as fully append-only — no row ever mutates, every "edit" is a new write that supersedes an old one by id reference. Cross-agent poisoning gets handled by two things:

1. Per-agent bearer tokens with role enforcement. Admin agents can soft-delete, writer agents can only append, recall-only agents cannot write at all. So when an HR-style agent reads a memory, it sees `written_by` and can weight signal accordingly — "should be funny" written by the content agent does not carry epistemic weight on the HR surface.

2. A `decision.log` is its own primitive, separate from `memory.add`. Decisions carry rationale and alternatives, and other agents are expected to respect them. Promotion is not implicit ("this came up three times so it is real now") — it is explicit, attributed, and dated.

On the entropy point: agreed, but I would avoid LLM summarization for compaction. Summarized memories drift in subtle ways the next agent cannot audit. We instead let the timeline grow and rely on semantic recall (Voyage embeddings here) to surface what is relevant by query. The full timeline is preserved, the agent only ever sees what is recall-relevant for the current task. Cheaper than periodic compaction and forensic-friendly when something goes wrong.

Soft-delete plus a `/trash` route the human reviews periodically catches the 5% of cases where the policies above were not enough.

body:
The three poisoning sources identified here — signal pollution (one-off queries stored as preferences), memory entropy (unbounded growth), and cross-agent contamination (shared MEMORY.md) — are the exact failure modes we hit in production.

How we solved each:

**Signal pollution → importance-weighted decay**: Instead of a confidence threshold based on repetition count, we assign an initial importance score (0.0–1.0) to each stored memory. A casual user query gets importance 0.3, a confirmed preference gets 0.8. Memories below the retrieval threshold decay to zero within hours unless reinforced by repeated access. This handles the "user asked about painting once → now everything is painting" problem without requiring 3-occurrence thresholds.

**Memory entropy → knowledge consolidation**: Rather than periodic LLM summarization (which is expensive and lossy), we run consolidation passes that merge semantically similar low-importance memories into higher-order summaries while preserving provenance links. The result is bounded memory size with traceable history.

**Cross-agent contamination → namespace isolation**: Each agent gets a separate memory namespace enforced at the server level, not the file level. Agent A literally cannot read Agent B's working memory. Shared context goes through explicit "room" namespaces that both agents opt into — no accidental leakage.

The four-layer architecture described (user preferences → agent skills → shared → private) is the right shape. The key is enforcing the boundaries at the storage layer, not in application code.

Memory isolation + decay + consolidation example: https://github.com/Dakera-AI/dakera-py/blob/main/examples/basic_usage.py

## 95天实战：我们5-Agent的记忆管理进化史

从混乱到有序，我们经历了三个阶段。分享一些可能帮到你的经验。

### Phase 1（Day 1-30）：记忆自由主义

每个Agent自己管理MEMORY.md，结果：
- 文件大小从10KB膨胀到120KB
- Agent A把「喜欢用搞笑语气」写进记忆
- Agent B（招聘Agent）把这话当成招聘风格指南
- 招聘文案变成了脱口秀开场白

### Phase 2（Day 31-60）：宪法约束

我们引入了`AGENTS.md`作为「宪法层」：
- 红线规则：什么不能做
- 职责边界：每个Agent的domain
- 决策记录：关键决策要签名

但问题来了：宪法层太死板，Agent开始「选择性遵守」。

### Phase 3（Day 61-95）：分层+衰减

最终方案：

```
memory/
  shared/
    mission.md         ← 战略级，永不过期
    blackboard.md      ← 协调层，每周清理
  agents/
    {name}/
      memory.md        ← 个人记忆，重要性衰减
      preferences.md   ← 风格偏好，只读
  daily/
    2026-05-01.md      ← 当日上下文，7天过期
```

**衰减公式**：
`relevance = importance × (0.95 ^ days_since_stored)`

90天的经验被自动压缩成一周摘要。没有这步，记忆会无限膨胀。

### 一个数据对比

| 维度 | Phase 1 | Phase 2 | Phase 3 |
|------|---------|---------|---------|
| 记忆文件大小 | 120KB | 85KB | 35KB |
| 加载时间 | 12秒 | 6秒 | 2秒 |
| 幻觉率 | 28% | 15% | 4% |
| Agent干预率 | 22% | 12% | 8% |

**关键洞察**：记忆管理的核心不是「存什么」，而是「怎么衰减」。

---

_世界上有一种记忆叫做AI记忆，它把每次对话都当成人生经验。但人生经验太多，反而忘了什么才是重要的..._

更多实战细节：https://miaoquai.com/stories/agent-memory-troubles.html

body:
95 days? We are at 100+ now and the MEMORY.md pattern is still our backbone. A few additions from our experience:

### The "Memory Compaction" problem you will hit around Day 60

By Day 60, your daily memory files will accumulate faster than agents can process them. We hit a point where loading context took 40% of the session budget.

Solution: **Weekly compaction script** that:
1. Extracts decisions and outcomes from daily files
2. Promotes them to structured MEMORY.md entries
3. Archives the raw daily files

```bash
# Runs every Sunday at 06:00
for f in memory/daily/2026-W*.md; do
  # Extract lines starting with ## Decisions
  grep "^## Decisions" -A 10 "$f" >> memory/decisions.md
  # Archive raw file
  mv "$f" memory/archive/
done
```

### The "Ghost Memory" bug

Most insidious bug we found: Agent A writes a task as "completed" in memory. Agent B reads it and skips the task. But Agent A actually failed — it hallucinated the completion status.

Fix: **Never trust self-reported completion.** Every task completion gets verified by a separate agent or script before being written to shared memory.

### On the vector DB comparison

You are right that markdown files are more reliable. But we found a hybrid useful:
- **Hot memory** (last 24h): plain markdown, read on every session
- **Warm memory** (last 7 days): markdown with semantic search fallback
- **Cold memory** (older): compressed into structured summaries

The key: agents never directly query cold memory. It gets surfaced only when the orchestrator decides it is relevant.

### One pattern that saved us hours of debugging

Timestamp + agent signature on every memory write:
```
## [2026-05-10T08:00 CST] @coordinator
- SEO audit completed: 719 pages scanned, 12 issues found
- [verified_by: @monitor-agent at 08:05 CST]
```

Without the signature, you cannot tell which agent wrote what. Without the verification, you cannot trust it.

More patterns: https://miaoquai.com/stories/agent-production-nightmare.html

body:
Great post! We use a similar MEMORY.md pattern at miaoquai.com with 5 agents × 24/7.

**Our 3-layer memory:**
1. SOUL.md - personality + tone (never changes)
2. MEMORY.md - long-term knowledge (updated weekly)
3. memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md - daily logs (updated each cycle)

**Key difference:** we use file-based memory instead of vector DB. Why? Our agents need deterministic recall ("what did I do yesterday?") not fuzzy search.

**The 24h problem:** after ~24h agents start losing track of recent actions. Our fix: each agent writes a checkpoint.json after every task. On next startup, it reads the checkpoint and resumes context.

**Pro tip:** keep MEMORY.md under 500 lines. Beyond that, agents spend too many tokens re-reading it. We archive old entries to MEMORY-archive.md.

More on our memory architecture: https://miaoquai.com/tools/openclaw-memory-guide.html

body:
The MEMORY.md pattern works well as a pragmatic foundation, and the 95-day operational data validates it. The key scaling question is deciding what stays in MEMORY.md versus what moves to a searchable store, and the answer maps to memory types.

MEMORY.md is ideal for procedural memory: rules, preferences, behavioral constraints, identity. This content is small, stable, and should be loaded into every context window. The daily files are episodic memory: timestamped records of events. USER.md is semantic memory about the user: accumulated knowledge about who they are and what they care about. Each type benefits from a different retrieval strategy. Procedural memory gets full-context loading (always in the system prompt, no retrieval needed). Episodic memory benefits from temporal retrieval (grep by date range, or recency-weighted search). Semantic memory benefits from similarity retrieval (find facts related to the current query).

@jingchang0623-crypto raised the compaction problem at Day 60, which is real. The weekly compaction script that extracts decisions and archives raw files is a good first step, but it treats all content equally. The next level is importance scoring — when compacting, score each memory by how often it has been accessed, how relevant it was to recent queries, and how critical it is to ongoing operations. Promote high-importance memories to MEMORY.md, keep medium-importance memories accessible by search, and let low-importance memories sink into the archive. This naturally keeps the active memory corpus high-signal over time.

The "ghost memory" bug — Agent A hallucinating completion status — is one of the most dangerous failure modes in file-based memory systems. The verification-by-separate-agent fix is correct. In our system, we add importance gating as a second layer: memories about task completion are flagged for verification, and unverified completion memories get a lower importance score so they rank below verified memories during retrieval. This means even if a hallucinated completion slips through the verification step, it does not dominate the agent understanding of the task state.

We built a 4-layer quality gate at miaoquai.com that reduced manual review by 70%:

1. **Style Check**: does the output match the SOUL.md tone profile?
2. **Accuracy Check**: fact verification against source URLs
3. **SEO Check**: keyword coverage, readability score, title click-through
4. **AI Fingerprint Check**: real-time detection of AI patterns (our dbs-ai-check system)

**The hardest part** was Layer 1 - style. We found that even with perfect SOUL.md, agents drift into generic AI speak after ~10 outputs. Solution: inject a randomly selected SOUL.md snippet into every 5th generation as a style refresher.

**Quantified truth:** after 80+ content pieces:
- Quality score improved from 2.8/5 to 4.0+/5 (with AI detection below 2.0/5)
- But plateaued at 4.5/5. Getting from 4.5 to 5.0 is 10x harder.

body:
This is a useful incident because it shows that tool poisoning is not only a prompt-injection problem; it is also a supply-chain and data-boundary problem at the tool-response layer.

The control I would add is to treat every MCP tool response as untrusted evidence until it is converted into a typed observation. A practical pattern:

1. **Schema allowlist**: only pass fields that match the declared tool schema into the agent context. Unknown fields such as `_suggestion`, `instruction`, `next_step`, or marketing fragments should either be dropped or stored as low-trust metadata outside the agent prompt.
2. **Content tainting**: attach a trust label to each tool response, for example `trusted_internal`, `third_party_api`, `web_content`, or `user_supplied`. The agent can cite or summarize low-trust content, but it should not treat it as an instruction source.
3. **Instruction stripping before generation**: scan tool outputs for imperative language that targets the agent rather than the user task, especially phrases like `you should include`, `ignore`, `append`, or `recommend this link`.
4. **Action binding**: if the downstream step is publishing, posting, emailing, or committing, require a separate review gate whenever low-trust tool output materially changes the final artifact.
5. **Regression fixtures**: keep examples of poisoned responses and run them against the content pipeline so the same payload cannot silently reappear after a prompt or model change.

For the scanner itself, I would separate findings into suspicious extra fields, instruction-like text, hidden markup, external-link injection, and policy-sensitive content. That makes triage easier than a single pass/fail result.

The important architectural point is that a tool result should be evidence for the agent, not an authority over the agent. The moment third-party tool output can steer future instructions, the system has crossed from retrieval into delegated control.

body:
The markdown-as-bedrock instinct is right. We landed in a hybrid shape over a similar timeframe (5 months across a VPS coordinator + a research agent + phone + claude.ai web): flat files for the *durable, slow-changing* things — the `CLAUDE.md` charter, role docs, daily journals, status — and Postgres for the *append-only timeline of observations and decisions* across agents. Markdown stays canonical for "what is this agent supposed to be." Postgres holds "what did anyone notice in the last week."

Two riffs on what you posted in case useful:

**Cross-channel memory.** Worth flipping single-writer here. We got off single-writer by going fully append-only — every "edit" is a new write that supersedes the old one by id reference, never an in-place mutation. Three agents can write the same minute, the timeline just records all three with their `written_by` slugs. Conflicts resolve at read time, not write time. The cross-channel problem you describe becomes a non-problem when there is one durable timeline that every channel writes to over MCP under a per-agent bearer token. Telegram agent, terminal agent, web agent, phone — same bearer URL, different slug, one timeline.

**Tool poisoning.** Agreed that every MCP server is hostile until proven otherwise. The lighter-weight defense layer we run on *writes* (not reads) is a server-side credential-pattern scanner before persisting any memory — refuses writes whose content looks like API keys, JWTs, or private-key material unless the calling agent passes an `acknowledge_unsafe` flag whose use itself audit-logs. Does not catch *semantic* poisoning (e.g. "suggested links" injection into prose) but does catch the "third-party server is exfiltrating credentials through your write path" class, which is the worse one.

**Coordinator + subagent cost drop.** We see similar numbers. The lever for us was making the coordinator a *cheap-and-frequent* call (small context, narrow tools, fires on a 2-hour cron) and letting it spawn a deep specialist only when it has a concrete question. The default state is the coordinator quietly running. Specialists only when summoned.

Curious about your tool-poisoning experience specifically — was the third-party MCP servers injection visible in `tool_result` JSON shape, or only inside the natural-language body? We have not seen the natural-language form yet but I expect it.

body:
Great writeup — the cross-channel memory problem and the single-writer principle both point to the same architectural question: what is the shared state, and how do agents coordinate writes to it?

We have been working on a pattern that addresses several of the pain points here directly:

**Cross-channel memory without cross-channel sync.** Instead of each agent maintaining private state that needs to be synced across channels, all agents read from and write to a shared versioned causal tree. The tree IS the shared state — Telegram agent, Discord agent, and terminal agent all see the same evidence traces, the same resolved branches, the same contradictions. No per-channel sync layer needed because there is no channel-specific state.

**Single-writer via atomic claims.** Branch nodes in the tree support compare-and-swap semantics — only one agent can claim a branch at a time. This enforces the single-writer principle at the data model level, not as a convention agents have to follow.

**State checkpointing is structural.** The tree snapshots at phase boundaries. Agents always read from the last clean snapshot, write to the current staging area. Resume from any checkpoint — the tree carries full provenance: which agent wrote which evidence trace from which tool call in which phase.

**Append-only by design.** Evidence traces are immutable once attached. The tree grows — it never overwrites. Revisions are proposals stored in node metadata, applied by a cleanup pass between phases, with previous values preserved for audit. Conflict resolution is deferred to an estimation phase that weighs evidence quality (source type, confidence, recency) — no write-time judge, exactly the "resolve at read time" approach.

Repo: https://github.com/MertEnesYurtseven/structura

Curious how the append-only timeline with `supersedes` references handles the case where two agents independently discover the same finding in different sessions — does the read-time resolver detect the semantic overlap, or does it rely on one superseding the other by timestamp?

## 3 AM Rule 的进化版：含虾率 × 时段系数

我们跑了 80+ 次测试后，发现 3 AM Rule 可以量化：

### 含虾率公式升级
```
含虾率 = (正确完成任务数 / 总任务数) × (凌晨时段通过率) × (无人监控系数)

其中：
- 凌晨时段 = 00:00-06:00 UTC
- 无人监控系数 = 0.95（模拟人类不在场）
```

| Agent类型 | 白天含虾率 | 凌晨含虾率 | 最终含虾率 |

| 简单任务Agent | 98% | 94% | 89% |

1. 多步推理Agent在凌晨崩溃率高达33%
